basic_info: 52-year-old male presenting with headaches and a pituitary mass
present_illness: Headaches for a few months, with a pituitary mass discovered. The patient reports bumping into door frames, suggesting possible visual field deficits. No hormonal imbalances or fatigue reported. The mass was discovered during an MRI and is pressing on the optic chiasm. The patient hasn’t had any other treatments for it yet, just the initial tests. Headaches are located behind the eyes, described as a dull, nagging ache, worsening over the past few months from a 3 out of 10 to a 6 out of 10, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time. The patient has not noticed changes in peripheral vision but has been bumping into door frames, which the doctor attributed to vision loss. The patient has not noticed changes in his sense of smell, and he has not had double vision or balance issues. The patient has been diagnosed with bitemporal hemianopia, as confirmed by the neurological examination, and visual field testing is pending.
past_history: No relevant past medical history, no prior surgeries, no known allergies. Family history is unremarkable for similar conditions.
physical_exam: Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological examination reveals no focal deficits, but the patient reports bumping into door frames, suggesting possible bitemporal hemianopia. Cranial nerve examination shows no other abnormalities.
aux_exam: MRI of the brain with contrast showed a pituitary mass compressing the optic chiasm. Pituitary hormone blood tests revealed low TSH, with other hormones within normal limits. Visual field testing is pending and scheduled before surgery. Exact dimensions of the pituitary mass are not available to the patient, but it is described as significant enough to compress the optic chiasm.
